A.title: APPENDIX A: MASTER INDEX OF COMPARISON TABLES, AND EXTRA COMPARISONS
A.rawText:
The tables below are placed next to the concepts they compare. This index
tells you where to find each one, followed by a few additional comparisons
of frequently confused ideas.

A.1 INDEX OF COMPARISON TABLES
  Comparison                               Where
  Scalar vs vector vs matrix               Module 6.1
  Linear independence vs dependence        Module 8.3
  Eigenvalues vs singular values           Module 10.6 (preview at 9.6)
  Differentiation vs integration           Module 3.10 (preview), Module 4 end
  Definite vs indefinite integral          Module 4 (end)
  Separable vs linear first-order ODEs     Module 16 (end)
  Searching methods; data-structure costs  Modules 17.6, 18.6
  Stack vs queue                           Module 18.4
  Binary heap vs binary search tree        Module 19.2
  Sorting algorithms                       Module 20.3
  Recursion vs iteration                   Module 22.3
  SIMD vs MIMD; parallel vs concurrent;    Modules 28.5, 28.6, 28.7
   shared vs distributed memory
  Mean vs median vs mode                   Module 29.5
  Population vs sample variance            Module 31.2
  Covariance vs correlation                Module 32 (end)
  Permutations vs combinations             Module 33.5
  Sampling with vs without replacement     Module 33.6
  Mutually exclusive vs independent        Module 34.2
  PMF vs PDF vs CDF                        Module 35.4
  Discrete vs continuous random variables  Module 35.4
  Standard deviation vs standard error     Module 37.6
  Unbiased vs consistent                   Module 37.5
  Type I vs Type II error                  Module 39.5
  z-test vs t-test                         Module 39.7
  Simple vs multiple regression            Module 40.2
  Outlier vs leverage vs influence         Module 40.5
  Gradient descent vs Newton's method      Module 43.4
  Gini vs entropy                          Module 44.3
  Classification vs regression trees       Module 44.1; vs regression: 48
  Single tree vs random forest             Module 45.5
  Bagging vs boosting                      Module 45.1
  Training error vs test error             Module 46.1
  Parameters vs hyperparameters            Module 47.1
  Grid vs random search                    Module 47.3
  Bootstrap vs cross-validation            Module 47.5
  Method of moments vs MLE                 Module 38.4
  Decision trees vs linear classifiers     Module 48.3
  Classification vs regression             Module 48 (start)
  Loss functions for classification        Module 48.7

A.2 ADDITIONAL COMPARISONS
  (a) PROBABILITY vs LIKELIHOOD
    Aspect          Probability                       Likelihood
    Question        how plausible are DATA given a    how plausible is a PARAMETER given
                    fixed parameter?                  fixed data?
    Varies          the data x                        the parameter theta
    Notation        P(x | theta) or f(x; theta)       L(theta) = f(x_observed; theta)
    Sums/integrates to 1 over x                       NOT 1 over theta (not a distribution)
    Use             prediction, simulation            estimation (MLE), model comparison
  (b) CONFIDENCE INTERVAL vs PREDICTION INTERVAL vs CREDIBLE INTERVAL
    Aspect          Confidence int.            Prediction int.             Credible int. (Bayes)
    About           a parameter (mean, slope)  one NEW observation         a parameter
    Width shrinks   with n toward 0            not below the noise level   with n and prior
    With n          yes                        no (stays about +/-2 sigma) yes
    Meaning         95% of such intervals      95% of future values        95% posterior prob.
                    cover the parameter        fall inside                 parameter is inside
    Where           Module 39.6                Module 40.1 (F40.5)         Module 38 (Bayes note)
  (c) PEARSON CORRELATION vs REGRESSION SLOPE
    Aspect          Correlation r                      Slope b_1 (y on x)
    Units           none                               units of y per unit of x
    Symmetry        r(x, y) = r(y, x)                  b_1(y on x) differs from b_1(x on y)
    Relation        r = b_1 s_x/s_y                    b_1 = r s_y/s_x
    Tells           strength + direction of linear     how much y changes per unit x
                    association
    Changes under   invariant to positive rescaling    scales inversely with x units
    rescaling       of x or y
  (d) STANDARDIZATION vs MIN-MAX NORMALIZATION vs ROBUST SCALING
    Module 42.6 (F42.1): z = (x - mean)/sd; (x - min)/(max - min); (x - median)/IQR.
  (e) INTERPOLATION vs EXTRAPOLATION
    Prediction inside the range of the training data (usually reliable) vs
    outside it (unreliable: linear fits can exceed physical limits, trees
    become constant, polynomials explode). See F40.5.
  (f) VARIANCE vs STANDARD DEVIATION vs STANDARD ERROR vs MSE
    Var: average squared deviation (squared units); SD: its square root (data
    units); SE: SD of an ESTIMATOR (sigma/sqrt n); MSE of an estimator =
    Var + Bias^2; MSE of a model = average squared prediction error.
  (g) FREQUENTIST vs BAYESIAN VIEW (outline)
    Frequentist: parameters fixed, probability = long-run frequency over
    repeated samples (p-values, CIs). Bayesian: parameters have probability
    distributions (prior -> posterior via Bayes' theorem); probability =
    degree of belief. Both agree for large samples and weak priors.

B.title: APPENDIX B: SYMBOL AND NOTATION GLOSSARY
B.rawText:
GREEK LETTERS (as written in plain text)
  alpha      significance level; learning-rate-like constant; Type I error
             probability; Lagrange/dual coefficients in SVM
  beta       regression coefficient; Type II error probability
  gamma      RBF kernel parameter; discount factor; skewness (gamma_1)
  delta      small change or difference (Delta, delta); delta function;
             discriminant function delta_k (LDA)
  epsilon    small positive number (limits); error term in regression (eps)
  eta        learning rate (step size)
  theta      generic parameter (vector); angle
  kappa      condition number
  lambda     eigenvalue; rate of exponential/Poisson; regularization strength;
             Lagrange multiplier
  mu         population mean; mean vector; momentum coefficient
  nu         degrees of freedom (sometimes)
  pi         3.14159...; also prior class probability pi_k; product symbol Pi
  rho        population correlation; correlation between trees; radius
             (spherical coordinate); contraction coefficient (Nelder-Mead)
  sigma      population standard deviation; singular value; sigmoid sigma(z)
             (context decides); shrink coefficient (Nelder-Mead)
  Sigma      covariance matrix; sum symbol (capital Sigma)
  phi        feature map; polar angle in spherical coordinates; Phi = standard
             normal CDF
  omega, Omega  an outcome; the sample space
  xi         slack variable (SVM); unknown point between a and x (Taylor)

GENERAL MATHEMATICAL SYMBOLS
  sum[i=1..n]        summation              prod[i=1..n]    product
  |x|                absolute value (scalar) or Euclidean norm (vector)
  |A| or det(A)      determinant (context); |A|_F Frobenius norm
  A^T, A^(-1), A^+   transpose, inverse, pseudo-inverse
  tr(A)              trace (sum of diagonal)
  I                  identity matrix; 1 a vector of ones
  R, R^n, R^(m x n)  real numbers; n-dim real vectors; m x n real matrices
  N, Z, Q            natural numbers, integers, rationals
  in, subset         is an element of; is a subset of
  U, n (cap)         union, intersection ("n" written for the intersection
                     symbol when the context is sets/events)
  empty set          {} or the symbol for no elements
  =>, <=>            implies; if and only if
  approx             approximately equal to; ~ "is distributed as" (X ~ N(0,1))
  lim, sup, inf      limit, supremum (least upper bound), infimum or infinity
                     (context: "inf" also means infinity in this document)
  argmin, argmax     argument at which the minimum/maximum occurs
  d/dx, f'(x)        derivative; partial f/partial x: partial derivative
  grad f, nabla f    gradient; H Hessian; J Jacobian
  int[a..b]          definite integral from a to b
  n!                 factorial; C(n,k) binomial coefficient; P(n,k) permutations
  floor(x), ceil(x)  round down, round up
  mod                remainder after division; // floor division in Python
  O(.), Omega(.), Theta(.)   asymptotic upper, lower, tight bounds
  ln, log, log2      natural, base-10 (or generic), base-2 logarithms
  e                  Euler's number 2.71828...
  i                  imaginary unit sqrt(-1) (also an index; context)

PROBABILITY AND STATISTICS
  P(A), P(A|B)       probability, conditional probability
  A^c                complement of A
  X, Y               random variables; x, y their values or data
  p(x), f(x), F(x)   PMF, PDF, CDF
  E[X], Var(X), Cov(X,Y), sd(X)   expectation, variance, covariance, SD
  x_bar, s, s^2      sample mean, SD, variance; p_hat sample proportion
  mu, sigma, sigma^2 population mean, SD, variance; rho population correlation
  theta_hat          estimator/estimate of theta; b (b_j) regression estimates
  SE                 standard error; df degrees of freedom
  H0, H1             null and alternative hypotheses
  alpha, beta, 1-beta   Type I error rate, Type II error rate, power
  Z, T               standard normal and t statistics; z, t their observed values
  N(mu, sigma^2)     normal distribution with mean mu and VARIANCE sigma^2
  U(a,b), Exp(lambda), Bin(n,p), Bernoulli(p), Poisson(lambda)
  iid                independent and identically distributed
  L(theta), l(theta) likelihood, log-likelihood; I(theta) Fisher information
  SSE, SSR, SST, R^2 sums of squares; coefficient of determination
  TP, FP, FN, TN     confusion-matrix counts
  CV                 cross-validation; OOB out-of-bag

COMPUTER SCIENCE
  n                  input size; T(n) running time; S(n) space
  DFA, NFA           deterministic / nondeterministic finite automaton
  Sigma              alphabet (formal languages); Sigma* all finite strings;
                     eps the empty string; L(M) language of machine M
  O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n^2), O(2^n), O(n!)  growth classes
  SIMD, MIMD, SISD, MISD   Flynn's taxonomy
  PK, FK             primary key, foreign key; sigma, pi, x (relational algebra:
                     selection, projection, Cartesian product; written by name)

DATA SCIENCE AND ML
  X (n x p)          design/feature matrix (rows = samples)
  y                  target vector; y_hat predictions
  w, b               weights and bias; beta regression coefficients
  eta                learning rate; C inverse regularization (SVM, sklearn
                     logistic regression); K kernel; gamma RBF parameter
  G, H               Gini impurity, entropy (tree context)
  B                  number of trees / bootstrap replicates; m features per split
  kappa              condition number lambda_max/lambda_min

D.title: APPENDIX D: SUPPLEMENTARY TOPICS RECOMMENDED BY THE SYLLABUS (SECTION 5)
D.rawText:
[SUPPLEMENTARY] The syllabus (section 5) suggests six extensions beyond the
university assessment. They are NOT part of the 48 modules, so this appendix
gives only orientation and the few formulas that earlier modules refer to
(KL divergence, KKT conditions, log-sum-exp). Nothing here replaces a full
course.

D.1 INFORMATION THEORY (entropy, KL divergence, cross-entropy, mutual
    information)
  F-D.1  ENTROPY, CROSS-ENTROPY, KL DIVERGENCE, MUTUAL INFORMATION
  B. FORMULAS (discrete distributions P, Q on the same outcomes; natural log
     gives nats, log2 gives bits)
       Entropy:            H(P) = - sum_x P(x) ln P(x)
       Cross-entropy:      H(P, Q) = - sum_x P(x) ln Q(x)
       KL divergence:      KL(P || Q) = sum_x P(x) ln( P(x)/Q(x) ) = H(P, Q) - H(P)
       Mutual information: I(X; Y) = sum_(x,y) P(x,y) ln( P(x,y)/(P(x)P(y)) )
                                    = KL( P(x,y) || P(x) P(y) ) = H(X) - H(X | Y)
  C. SYMBOLS: P the "true" (or reference) distribution; Q the model
     distribution; P(x,y) joint; P(x), P(y) marginals.
  D. CONCEPT: entropy = average uncertainty/surprise of P (the node impurity of
     F44.3). Cross-entropy = average surprise if you code outcomes drawn from
     P using a model Q: the log-loss of classification (Module 46/48).
     KL divergence = the EXTRA surprise caused by using Q instead of P; it is
     >= 0, equals 0 iff P = Q, and is NOT symmetric and not a distance.
     Mutual information = how much knowing one variable reduces
     uncertainty about the other: it detects ANY dependence (including
     XOR-like nonlinear dependence) and is zero iff independent.
  E. CONDITIONS: Q(x) > 0 wherever P(x) > 0 (else KL is infinite); continuous
     versions use integrals (differential entropy can be negative).
  G. EXAMPLES
     P = (0.5, 0.5), Q = (0.9, 0.1):
       H(P) = ln 2 = 0.6931 nats (1 bit).
       KL(P || Q) = 0.5 ln(0.5/0.9) + 0.5 ln(0.5/0.1) = 0.5(-0.5878) + 0.5(1.6094)
                  = 0.5108.
       KL(Q || P) = 0.9 ln(1.8) + 0.1 ln(0.2) = 0.5290 - 0.1609 = 0.3681
                  (different: asymmetric).
       H(P, Q) = -0.5 ln 0.9 - 0.5 ln 0.1 = 0.0527 + 1.1513 = 1.2040
                = H(P) + KL(P || Q) = 0.6931 + 0.5108. OK.
     CLASSIFICATION: for a one-hot true label (P puts probability 1 on the true
       class) the cross-entropy reduces to -ln Q(true class): predicting
       probability 0.7 for the right class costs -ln 0.7 = 0.357 nats. Averaging
       over data gives log-loss (F46.5). Minimizing cross-entropy = maximizing
       likelihood = minimizing KL to the empirical distribution (F38.3).
     Mutual information: joint P(0,0) = P(1,1) = 0.4, P(0,1) = P(1,0) = 0.1,
       marginals (0.5, 0.5): I = 2(0.4) ln(0.4/0.25) + 2(0.1) ln(0.1/0.25)
       = 0.376 - 0.183 = 0.1927 nats (0.278 bits). For independent variables
       I = 0.
  H. USES: tree splits (information gain = mutual information between the
     feature split and the class), feature selection (mutual_info_classif),
     variational inference, t-SNE/UMAP objectives, knowledge distillation.

D.2 OPTIMIZATION THEORY: LAGRANGE MULTIPLIERS AND KKT CONDITIONS
  Convex sets: C is convex if the segment between any two of its points lies in
  C. A convex optimization problem (convex f, convex feasible set) has no
  spurious local minima (F43.1).
  Constrained problem:  minimize f(x) subject to g_i(x) <= 0, h_j(x) = 0.
  Lagrangian: L(x, mu, lambda) = f(x) + sum_i mu_i g_i(x) + sum_j lambda_j h_j(x).
  KARUSH-KUHN-TUCKER (KKT) CONDITIONS (necessary at a regular optimum; sufficient
  for convex problems):
     1. Stationarity:       grad f + sum mu_i grad g_i + sum lambda_j grad h_j = 0
     2. Primal feasibility: g_i(x) <= 0, h_j(x) = 0
     3. Dual feasibility:   mu_i >= 0
     4. Complementary slackness: mu_i g_i(x) = 0 (an inactive constraint has
        multiplier 0; an active one may have a positive multiplier)
  EXAMPLE: minimize x^2 + y^2 subject to x + y >= 2, i.e. g = 2 - x - y <= 0.
     Stationarity: (2x, 2y) + mu(-1, -1) = 0 -> x = y = mu/2. The constraint is
     active (x + y = 2) -> x = y = 1, mu = 2 >= 0, f = 2. All four KKT
     conditions hold (convex problem: global minimum).
     Equality case (F12.8): maximize xy subject to x + y = 10: x = y = 5.
  Where it appears: SVM dual (the KKT conditions say alpha_i > 0 only for
  support vectors, F48.6), regularization as a constraint (ridge: |w|^2 <= t
  corresponds to a penalty lambda), PCA (maximize a quadratic form on the unit
  sphere), maximum entropy models.

D.3 NUMERICAL MATHEMATICS: STABILITY AND ERROR
  Key ideas: floating-point rounding (machine epsilon 2.2e-16 for float64);
  absorption and catastrophic cancellation (Module 26, 41.7); conditioning
  of a problem (condition number: amplification of input errors, F10.7);
  stability of an algorithm (small errors stay small); truncation error
  (approximating a series/derivative, F5.6, F43.2) vs round-off error;
  convergence rates of iterations (linear, quadratic: F43.3-F43.4).
  LOG-SUM-EXP TRICK (stable softmax and log-likelihood): ln sum_i e^(x_i) = m +
  ln sum_i e^(x_i - m), m = max_i x_i.
     Example: x = (1000, 1001): the naive e^1000 overflows (result inf);
     stable: 1001 + ln(e^(-1) + 1) = 1001.3133. Softmax = e^(x_i - m)/sum e^(x_j - m)
     = (0.2689, 0.7311).
  Other practices: solve linear systems with factorizations (LU, QR, Cholesky)
  not inverses; standardize variables; add small jitter or ridge terms to
  near-singular matrices; use log-probabilities instead of products; compare
  floats with tolerances.

D.4 REAL ANALYSIS (orientation)
  Rigorous foundations behind Modules 1-5: completeness of the reals (every
  bounded set has a least upper bound), epsilon-delta limits and continuity
  (F2.1), sequences (Cauchy sequences converge), series convergence,
  uniform vs pointwise convergence, differentiability vs continuity,
  the mean value theorem and Taylor's theorem with remainder (F5.6), Riemann
  integrability, interchanging limits with integrals/sums (dominated
  convergence). Skills: reading and writing epsilon-delta and induction
  proofs, constructing counter-examples (Level 3 of the syllabus).

D.5 ADVANCED PROBABILITY (orientation)
  - MODES OF CONVERGENCE of random variables: almost sure (strongest), in
    L^2/mean square, in probability, in distribution (weakest). Almost sure
    and L^2 convergence each imply convergence in probability, which
    implies convergence in distribution.
  - LAWS OF LARGE NUMBERS: weak (in probability, F37.3) and strong (almost surely).
  - CENTRAL LIMIT THEOREM (F37.4) and its extensions (Lindeberg, multivariate,
    delta method: Var(g(X_bar)) approx g'(mu)^2 sigma^2/n).
  - CONDITIONAL EXPECTATION E[X | Y] (a random variable). Tower property
    E[E[X | Y]] = E[X]; LAW OF TOTAL VARIANCE
        Var(X) = E[ Var(X | Y) ] + Var( E[X | Y] )
    (within-group + between-group, the same decomposition as F26.4;
    example: two equal groups with means 0 and 4 and variance 1 each:
    total variance = 1 + 4 = 5).
  - Moment generating and characteristic functions, joint/transformation
    of random vectors (Jacobian, F13.3), Markov chains (stationary
    distribution as an eigenvector, F9.2), Markov and Chebyshev inequalities,
    Jensen's inequality (F36.1), concentration bounds (Hoeffding).

D.6 MATHEMATICAL STATISTICS (orientation)
  SUFFICIENT STATISTICS (a statistic containing all information about the
  parameter; Fisher-Neyman factorization: f(x; theta) = g(T(x), theta) h(x)),
  the Rao-Blackwell theorem (conditioning an estimator on a sufficient
  statistic never increases variance), Cramer-Rao bound (F38.4), asymptotic
  normality of the MLE, likelihood-ratio, Wald and score tests (Neyman-
  Pearson lemma: the likelihood-ratio test is most powerful for simple
  hypotheses), Bayesian inference and conjugate priors (Beta-Bernoulli
  example, Module 38), exponential families and generalized linear models
  (linear, logistic and Poisson regression as special cases), robust
  statistics, nonparametric methods (rank tests, bootstrap, permutation
  tests, kernel density estimation).

D.7 SUGGESTED USE OF THIS DOCUMENT (from the syllabus: study-time suggestions)
  The syllabus proposes (not an official requirement) roughly 35%
  Mathematics, 30% Probability and Statistics, 15% Computer Science, 20%
  Data Science/ML, and the order: algebra and calculus -> linear algebra ->
  multivariable calculus and ODEs -> probability -> statistics and
  inference -> optimization and programming -> ML and validation, with
  computer science revision alongside. Levels of mastery: Level 1
  familiarity; Level 2 competence (solve independently, derive results,
  state assumptions); Level 3 depth (proofs, counter-examples, limitations,
  connections). Aim for Level 2 across the core and Level 3 in selected
  foundations. Use the worked examples in this file as exercises: cover the
  solution, solve, then compare.

F.title: APPENDIX F: FINAL QUALITY-CHECK RECORD
F.rawText:
This appendix records what was checked before the document was finalized,
and what the reader should still treat with care.

F.1 SIZE AND STRUCTURE
  Modules covered: 48 (Parts A-D of the syllabus), in syllabus order.
  Syllabus bullets listed in Appendix C: 410, each mapped to a section.
  Formula/rule blocks (IDs Fm.k): 236, indexed in Appendix E.
  Approximate length: 15379 lines, 124034 words (plain ASCII text).

F.2 THE QUALITY QUESTIONS (the nine questions of the task, plus two extra checks)
  1. Has every syllabus topic been covered?
     Yes: all 410 bullets are mapped in Appendix C. The mapping was made by
     keyword matching against each module and then reviewed by hand for the
     weak matches. One gap found in this review (substitutability and
     superclass/subclass terminology in Module 21) was added.
  2. Does every relevant formula have symbol explanations?
     Yes: every one of the 236 formula blocks has a lettered SYMBOLS part (C).
  3. Are the assumptions and restrictions explained?
     Yes: every block has a CONDITIONS part (E, 236 blocks); common mistakes
     are given in 234 blocks (I); a few table-style blocks (F5.4, F4.2)
     list their pitfalls in unlettered "COMMON MISTAKES" paragraphs.
  4. Are the worked examples mathematically correct?
     Checked as follows. (a) About 75 representative numerical statements
     from Modules 1-46 were recomputed with Python/NumPy/SciPy and all
     matched. (b) Every machine-learning experiment quoted (trees, forests,
     validation, leakage, tuning, SVM, LDA, kernels, lasso) was actually
     run with scikit-learn; the printed numbers are those results.
     (c) The code snippets for data structures, sorting and recursion were
     executed. (d) The remaining examples were computed by hand while
     writing. A reader who finds an arithmetic slip should correct it and
     treat it as a defect of this file, not of the topic.
  5. Are important concepts explained rather than merely named?
     Yes: each block has a CONCEPT part (D, 236 blocks) in plain English;
     interpretation (H) in 236 blocks; related formulas (J) in 236 blocks.
  6. Are confusing concepts compared?
     Yes: Appendix A indexes about 40 comparison tables (including all
     those requested in the task) plus extra comparisons.
  7. Are practical Data Science connections included?
     Yes: each module ends with or contains a DATA SCIENCE LINK, and Part D
     is built around realistic modeling workflows.
  8. Is the notation consistent?
     Conventions are fixed at the start and in Appendix B; where books
     differ (sample variance divisor, quartile rule, N(mu, sigma^2) versus
     scale, rate versus scale for the exponential, sklearn C versus
     lambda, row/column vectors, spherical coordinate symbols) the
     convention is stated where it is used.
  9. Are any sections incomplete or excessively compressed?
     See F.3 for the topics that are intentionally given at prerequisite
     depth, and for what is stated without proof.
 10. Cross-references: every formula ID mentioned in the text (for example
     F40.8) was checked automatically and exists in Appendix E.
 11. Format: plain ASCII only; mathematics in readable text notation;
     American spelling is used (syllabus bullets in Appendix C are quoted
     exactly as given, including their original spelling).

F.3 KNOWN LIMITS AND HOW TO USE THEM
  - FULL A-J TEMPLATE: derivations (part F) are given where they improve
    understanding (71 of 236 blocks), not for every elementary rule, as
    the task allows. Elementary rules use compressed parts.
  - DEPTH: Nelder-Mead, kernels/RBF, SVM, LDA, hypothesis-testing
    variants, and the Part B theory topics are treated at prerequisite
    (Level 2) depth. Theorems such as the CLT, Cramer-Rao bound,
    Eckart-Young, Fubini and the Halting problem are stated with the
    key idea of the proof rather than a complete rigorous proof.
  - NUMERICAL RESULTS FROM EXPERIMENTS depend on random seeds, library
    versions and the synthetic data used; the qualitative pattern is what
    matters. Rerun the code to reproduce.
  - STATSMODELS: its summary output was not executed in the environment
    used to prepare this file (library not installed); the coefficients,
    standard errors, t-values and R^2 quoted come from an independent
    hand-written OLS and match what statsmodels computes.
  - QUARTILES: the linear-interpolation rule (NumPy default) is used;
    other textbooks give slightly different Q1 and Q3 for small samples.
  - Plain-text tables are up to about 100 characters wide; use a monospaced
    font and no word wrap.
  - Study use: for each worked example, cover the solution, redo it by hand,
    then compare; for each formula, state its conditions from memory.
